claims.overstatement: None; the claim treats the review as second-hand and states the limits of its table. Wording points: (1) the review's single-dose statement (p. 10) concerns most cases of death or permanent neurological injury, reported in women aged 15 to 30, not most cases overall; its own table gives no amount for 14 of its 21 deaths (editors' count). (2) The table has two further faults the claim does not name: a fatal row cited only as '(2001)' with no author (traceable only through the anonymous first entry of the reference list, p. 12), and a row listed as methamphetamine whose cited paper's title names ecstasy (Salathe et al., 2018). (3) The review names sodium lost in sweat as a third mechanism alongside vasopressin release and drinking (abstract; p. 2) and calls the mechanisms not yet completely understood (p. 7); the claim's mechanism sentence leaves out the sweat route.
claims.note: Editors' counts recomputed from Table 3, every row checked on the rendered pages: 52 rows (1991-2018); 46 women, 6 men; 21 deaths, 27 recoveries, 3 outcomes 'Unknown', 1 blank; a sodium value in 36 rows, lowest per row 101 to 130 mmol/L (one man's row reads 137 on day one and 129 on day three); 10 deaths with a value, 109 to 126, inside the 101 to 130 of the 24 recoveries with a value; amount 'Unknown' in 29 rows and blank in 1 (30 of 52); 10 fatal rows cite Rosenson et al. (2007), whose title (p. 14) is the California series. Probable duplicates: two Matthai et al. (1996) rows (girls aged 15 and 16, sodium 119 and 112, both recovered) recur as Wilkins (1996), a BMJ letter on the same topic (reference, p. 14). Three fatal rows (Karlovsek et al. 2005, two; Libiseller et al. 2005) have no sodium value and no hyponatraemia among their listed effects. The O'Connor et al. (1999) row has amount, sodium and outcome blank although the reference title begins 'Death from hyponatraemia-induced cerebral oedema' (p. 14). Chen and Viola (1991), cited for a woman's case, is a laboratory method for detecting ras point mutations (Anal Biochem; reference, p. 13). The review's support for heavy drinking is described by its authors as anecdotal reports (p. 7); the only clubber study it cites (Aitchison et al., 2012) is cited for genetic variants, not intake.

anchors.extracted: 52 published cases with hyponatraemia after phenethylamines, 1991-2018: 46 women and 6 men; 21 deaths, 27 recoveries, 3 unknown, 1 blank; sodium given in 36 rows, lowest values 101-130 mmol/L; in the 10 deaths with a value, 109-126 mmol/L, within the 101-130 of the 24 recoveries with a value; amount taken unknown or blank in 30 rows (editors' counts).

anchors.locator: Table 3, Reference column; with the reference list, pp. 13-14
anchors.extracted: Table faults: Matthai 1996 cases (ages 15 and 16, sodium 119 and 112) repeated as Wilkins 1996 (a letter); Chen and Viola 1991 (a laboratory method paper on ras point mutations) cited for a woman's case; a fatal row cited only as '(2001)'; three fatal rows with no low sodium recorded (Karlovsek 2005 x2, Libiseller 2005); O'Connor 1999 row blank though the cited title reports a death; 10 of the 21 deaths from Rosenson et al. 2007 (California poison-centre series); Salathe 2018 listed as methamphetamine though its title names ecstasy.

Narrative review: PubMed searched until October 2019 with three term pairs (cathinone, amphetamine, MDMA each AND hyponatraemia) plus reference lists of retrieved papers; publications emphasising hyponatraemia, plasma sodium, cerebral oedema or nephrotoxicity considered; 168 publications reviewed; no appraisal or duplicate check described. One author was mainly responsible for the literature search and data collection (p. 12).

anchors.locator: Section 5.1.5 (Gender susceptibility and hormonal influence), 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: The review states, citing earlier reports, that most cases of death or permanent neurological injury from hyponatraemic encephalopathy were in women aged 15 to 30 after a single dose of MDMA. In its own Table 3 the amount is unknown for 14 of the 21 deaths (editors' count), so the table cannot check this.

anchors.locator: Abstract; Introduction, 3rd paragraph (p. 1, continuing on p. 2); Section 5, 2nd paragraph and Section 5.1, 1st paragraph (p. 7); Section 5.1.3, 1st paragraph (p. 10)
anchors.extracted: Mechanism as the review describes it: raised antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin) secretion through serotonin with water reabsorption by the kidney, excessive drinking, and sodium lost in sweat; over-hydration rests on what the authors call anecdotal reports (p. 7); mechanisms not yet completely understood (p. 7). The hormone rise is cited from volunteer studies (Henry et al., 1998: plasma ADH rose within 1-2 h after a low oral dose in healthy hydrated men, with a slight fall in sodium; p. 10), not measured by the review.

claims.overstatement: None; the claim marks the review as second-hand and its inference about women as resting on uncounted denominators. Precision points: 46 of 52 is 88.5%, which the review prints as 89% (p. 7); the review does not say the crossover study was in a laboratory (it says randomized placebo-controlled crossover in healthy volunteers); and its 'no significant differences ... in ADH or sodium' does not say whether between sexes or against placebo, an ambiguity the claim keeps. The 'after surgery' detail comes from the title of Ayus et al. (1992) in the review's reference list (p. 12), not from its text.
claims.note: Recomputed: 46/52 = 88.5%; without the two probable Wilkins duplicates of the Matthai cases, 44/50 = 88.0%. The 10 deaths from Rosenson et al. (2007) include 9 women. One woman's fatal row cites only '(2001)', with no author, and one woman's recovery cites Chen and Viola (1991), an unrelated laboratory-methods paper. No denominator (numbers of women and men using MDMA) appears anywhere in the review.

anchors.locator: Section 5, 1st paragraph (begins on p. 4; continued on p. 7 after Table 3)
anchors.extracted: Review: 89% of the Table 3 cases were young women, which it says indicates a probable predisposition of the female gender. Editors' count 46 of 52 (88.5%); 44 of 50 (88%) without two probable duplicates; no counts of women and men who use MDMA are set against these.

As described by the review (Simmler et al., 2011): randomized placebo-controlled crossover in 8 healthy men and 8 healthy women given MDMA 125 mg (study condition), plasma and urine osmolality, ADH and copeptin measured; copeptin (a marker of ADH secretion) rose in women but not in men; no significant differences in ADH or plasma sodium.

anchors.locator: Section 5.1.5, 2nd paragraph (p. 10, continuing on p. 11) and 3rd paragraph (p. 11)
anchors.extracted: Reasons offered for a higher risk in women: metabolic and hormonal factors; oestrogen lowering the osmotic threshold for ADH and increasing fluid retention (a study in women with suppressed reproductive hormones, no MDMA; rat studies); oestrogen inhibiting the sodium-potassium pump that protects brain cells; menstrual-cycle variation; lower muscle mass and body weight. None was tested in people who took MDMA.

anchors.locator: Section 5.1.5, 2nd paragraph; reference entry Ayus et al. (1992), p. 12
anchors.extracted: Review: once hyponatraemic encephalopathy develops, menstruant women are about 25 times more likely to die or have permanent brain injury than men or postmenopausal women (Ayus et al., 1992). The reference title (p. 12) shows the study was of postoperative hyponatraemic encephalopathy, not of drug use.

anchors.locator: Table 3, Gender and Reference columns; reference list pp. 13-14
anchors.extracted: The women's share rests on a table with probable duplicates (Matthai 1996 and Wilkins 1996, two girls), an unrelated laboratory-methods paper cited for a woman's case (Chen and Viola, 1991), an authorless fatal woman's row ('(2001)'), and 10 of its 21 deaths (9 women) taken from the California series (Rosenson et al., 2007).

key_findings.correction: Minor wording: the case with 137 mmol/L on day one and 129 on day three is one of the 36 rows with a sodium value (counted at its lowest, 129), not a further, 37th row; 36 with a value and 16 without make 52, as outcomes.operationalization says. The same parenthesis in analysis.effect_sizes needs the same change. All other counts confirmed (52 rows, 46 women, 6 men, ages 13-49, MDMA in 50, 21/27/3/1 outcomes, sodium 101-130, deaths 109-126).

reporting_issues.note: Checked on p. 12: the first reference entry is the anonymous 2001 Paediatr Child Health report, so the case is traceable through it.
Six rows list other substances (cannabinoids, benzodiazepines, promethazine with codeine, benzylpiperazine twice, insulin); concentrations in 4 rows.

risk_of_bias.note: Editors' narrative-review checklist, overall high, follows the worst domains; consistent with what this reader found in Table 3.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial. For gap (4), the specific count: the amount is unknown for 14 of the table's 21 deaths, and the review's single-dose statement is limited to deaths or permanent neurological injury in women aged 15 to 30 (p. 10).

missed: Table 3's first row (Salathe et al., 2018) lists the substance as methamphetamine, but the reference title (p. 14) is 'SIADH and water intoxication related to ecstasy'; its sodium and outcome are given as Unknown.
The 10 Rosenson et al. (2007) fatal rows include 9 women, so the California series also contributes to the women's share.
